title: LPIC-1 Exam 102 (102-500) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from the public LPIC-1 102-500 exam objectives (v5.0). Not real exam questions. Practice on your own lab machines (WSL, a VM or a cloud sandbox), never on production systems you don't manage, and scan or test only systems you own or have written permission to test.

q.q: A user's home folder holds ~/.bash_login and ~/.profile, but no ~/.bash_profile. The user opens a bash login shell over SSH. Which startup file does bash read from that group?
o: Both ~/.bash_login and ~/.profile, in that order
Bash does not read all of them. It stops at the first one it finds.
Only ~/.profile, because it is the most portable
~/.profile is the last choice in the list. It is used only when the other two are missing.
Only ~/.bashrc, because every bash session reads it first
A login shell does not read ~/.bashrc by itself. Many distributions add a line to ~/.profile that sources it, but that is not automatic.
Only ~/.bash_login
Right. Bash reads the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login and ~/.profile that exists and ignores the rest. Here that is ~/.bash_login.

q.q: Maria added alias ll='ls -lA' to ~/.bash_profile. She opens a terminal window inside her desktop session and the alias is missing. What is the most likely reason?
o: Aliases only work for the root account
Any user can define aliases for their own shell.
A terminal window opens a non-login shell, which reads ~/.bashrc only, not ~/.bash_profile
Right. ~/.bash_profile is for login shells. Put aliases in ~/.bashrc, or make ~/.bash_profile source ~/.bashrc.
Aliases cannot be defined in ~/.bash_profile, only on the command line
Aliases can be set in any startup file. The file just isn't read by this kind of shell.
~/.bash_profile is read only at shutdown
The file for shutdown-time commands is ~/.bash_logout, and it is read when a login shell exits.

q.q: You run: GREETING=hello and then bash -c 'echo "$GREETING"'. The second command prints an empty line. What fixes this while keeping the change in the current shell?
o: Add quotes around the word hello
Quotes do not change which processes can see the variable.
Run unset GREETING and set it again
Unsetting removes the variable. Setting it again without export gives the same result.
Run export GREETING after setting it, in the same shell
Right. The variable exists only in the current shell until it is exported. Exported variables are copied into child processes such as bash -c.
Use source GREETING in the child shell
source reads and runs a file. It is not a way to hand a variable to a child.

q.q: After editing ~/.bashrc, an admin wants the changes to apply in the shell that is already open, without logging out. Which command does that?
o: source ~/.bashrc
Right. source (or its short form a dot) runs the file's commands inside the current shell, so aliases and variables stay.
bash ~/.bashrc
This starts a child shell, runs the file there, and throws the changes away when the child exits.
export ~/.bashrc
export marks variables to be passed to children. It does not run a file.
exec ~/.bashrc
exec tries to replace the shell with the file as a program. The file is not an executable program, so it fails.

q.q: A company policy says each login shell must remove temporary files and clear the terminal when the user logs out. Which file is the standard place for those commands?
o: ~/.bash_exit
Bash has no startup or exit file by this name.
~/.bash_logout
Right. Bash reads this file when a login shell exits. It is the usual spot for clean-up commands.
/etc/profile.logout
No such system file is read by bash at logout.
~/.bashrc with a trap at the top
A trap in ~/.bashrc fires for every interactive shell, including non-login ones, so it would clean up at the wrong times.

q.q: The admin adds a file named .vimrc to /etc/skel. Who gets a copy?
o: Only accounts created later with a home folder, such as useradd -m
Right. /etc/skel is the template used when a new home folder is created. Existing users are not changed.
Every existing user at their next login
Nothing copies skel files to existing homes. Each existing user needs the file added by hand.
Only the root account
root's home is not built from /etc/skel at every login, and the template is meant for ordinary new users.
Every user on each reboot, which overwrites their own copy of the file
Skel is copied once, at account creation. No process refreshes it later.

q.q: You need a shortcut that creates a folder and then moves into it, used as: mkcd reports/2026. Which definition works in ~/.bashrc?
o: alias mkcd='mkdir -p $1 && cd $1'
An alias is plain text replacement. It has no $1, so the line would use an empty variable.
alias mkcd=mkdir -p; cd
The alias would hold only the first part, and the text after the semicolon would run as a separate command every time.
export mkcd='mkdir -p "$1" && cd "$1"'
export makes a variable, not a command, so typing mkcd would find nothing to run.
function mkcd { mkdir -p "$1" && cd "$1"; }
Right. A function can use positional parameters such as $1. The cd runs in your own shell, so you really move into the folder.

q.q: An admin wants to see only the variables that child processes will inherit. Which command prints just those?
o: set
set prints every shell variable and function, including ones that were never exported.
alias
alias lists defined aliases, which are not variables passed to children.
env
Right. env prints the exported environment. Programs started from the shell inherit exactly that list.
unset
unset removes variables and takes names as arguments. It does not list anything.

q.q: Which file is the right place to set an environment variable for the login shell of every user on the machine?
o: /etc/profile (or a script in /etc/profile.d/)
Right. This system-wide file is read by login shells of all users, so one change reaches everybody.
/etc/skel/.bash_profile, the template for new accounts
That is only a template for accounts created in the future. Existing users do not change.
~/.bash_profile of the admin
That file belongs to one user's home folder and affects only that user.
~/.bash_logout of root
That file runs when root's login shell ends, and it does not set anything for other users.

q.q: A script named backup.sh begins with #!/bin/bash and was saved from an editor. Running ./backup.sh prints 'Permission denied', though the file is in the current folder. What is the simplest fix?
o: Add a second line, #!/bin/sh, at the top
A shebang names the interpreter. It does not give the file permission to run.
Run source backup.sh as a normal user, then retry
source runs the commands in the current shell. It does not change the permissions of the file.
chmod u+x backup.sh
Right. To run a file directly the execute bit must be set. A new file made by an editor usually has only read and write.
Rename the file to backup.exe
Linux ignores file extensions when deciding if a file can run. Only the execute bit counts.

q.q: What does this command line print? true || echo A && echo B
o: A
echo A is skipped because true already returned success.
A and then B
|| does not run its right side when the left side succeeds, so A never prints.
Nothing, because the two operators cancel out
The operators do not cancel. They are checked left to right, and echo B runs.
B
Right. true succeeds, so the || branch is skipped. The && then sees a successful status from the whole left side and runs echo B.

q.q: What does the following loop print? for n in $(seq 2 3 11); do echo -n "$n "; done
o: That is every number from 2 to 11. seq would print it only with an increment of 1, but the middle argument is 3.
Right. seq takes first, increment, last. It starts at 2, adds 3 each time, and includes 11.
The first number is 2, so counting starts at 2, not at the step size.
11 is reached exactly (2 + 3 x 3) and seq includes the last value when it fits.

q.q: A script must skip a log file when it is empty (size 0 bytes) and process it otherwise. Which test is true only when the file exists and has a size greater than zero?
o: -e is true for any existing path, even a zero-byte file.
-z tests whether the string itself is empty. It never looks at the file's size.
Right. -s is true for an existing file that is not empty.
-d is true only for directories.

q.q: Which line stores today's date, like 2026-11-27, in a variable named stamp?
o: stamp=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
Right. $( ) runs the command and substitutes its output. Spaces around = would break the assignment, so there are none.
stamp=(date +%F)
Parentheses without a dollar sign build an array holding the two words date and +%F.
stamp='date +%F'
Single quotes keep the text literally, so the variable holds the words date +%F.
stamp = $(date +%F)
Spaces around = make bash treat stamp as a command name, which gives command not found.

q.q:
A script contains these lines. It never sends an alert, even when rsync fails. Why?
  rsync -a /data /backup
  echo "sync finished"
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then mail -s FAIL ops < /dev/null; fi
o: [ ] cannot compare numbers, so -ne is always false
-ne is a valid numeric test in [ ].
rsync always returns 0 in a script
rsync returns a non-zero code on errors, in scripts too.
The mail command must come before the if line
The order of the if and mail lines is not the problem. The tested value is.
$? holds the exit code of echo, not of rsync
Right. $? is overwritten by every command. Save it right after rsync, for example rc=$?, or test rsync directly in the if.

q.q: A script is run as: ./deploy.sh web01 prod. What does echo "$# $2 $0" print inside it?
o: 3 prod ./deploy.sh
$# does not count the script name, so the count is 2.
2 prod ./deploy.sh
Right. $# counts the arguments, $2 is the second argument, and $0 is the name the script was started with.
2 web01 deploy.sh
$2 is the second argument, which is prod. The first is $1. $0 keeps the path as typed.
2 prod web01
$0 is the script name, not the first argument.

q.q: A script ends with the line: exec /usr/local/bin/appserver --port 8080 and has a line echo 'launched' after it. What happens when the script runs?
o: appserver starts in the background and then 'launched' is printed
exec does not background anything. It also never returns to the script.
The script waits for appserver to finish, then prints 'launched'
That describes a plain command. exec never gives control back.
The shell is replaced by appserver, and the echo line never runs
Right. exec does not start a child. It swaps the running shell for the new program, so nothing after it executes.
The line fails because exec only accepts shell built-ins
exec can run any program on the system.

q.q: A script must ask the operator a question, show the text Continue (y/n)? on the same line, and keep the answer in a variable called ans. Which line does it?
o: read -r -p "Continue (y/n)? " ans
Right. read stores typed input in the named variable and -p shows a prompt first.
ans=read "Continue (y/n)? "
This sets ans to the word read and then tries to run the text as a command.
echo -p "Continue (y/n)? " > ans
echo only prints, and the redirect would write to a file named ans.
input ans "Continue (y/n)? "
input is not a bash command, so the shell says command not found.

q.q: An admin logs in to a Linux server by plain ssh from a Linux desktop and runs xclock. The program says it cannot open the display. Which change lets a window from the server appear on the desktop?
o: Run xhost + on the server
xhost controls who may connect to an X server. The display you want is the desktop's, so this is the wrong machine, and it opens it to everyone.
Copy /etc/X11/xorg.conf from the desktop to the server
The server has no screen to configure. The window must be drawn on the desktop's X server.
Start the server's session with startx
startx starts a local X session on a machine that has its own screen. A headless server would not show it on your desktop.
Reconnect with ssh -X to forward the display over SSH
Right. ssh -X turns on X11 forwarding. SSH sets DISPLAY on the server for you and carries the window data over the encrypted link.

q.q: You want an extra keyboard-layout setting for the X server on every login, without editing the main configuration file. Where does the setting belong?
o: A file named .xorg in each user's home folder
The X server reads its configuration from system folders, not from a hidden file in a home directory.
A .conf file inside /etc/X11/xorg.conf.d/
Right. The X server reads every .conf snippet in this folder. It keeps local settings separate from the package's own files.
/etc/X11/Xauthority
That name is not a configuration file for the server. Authorization cookies live in each user's ~/.Xauthority.
/etc/xdg/xorg.d/keyboard.sh
Shell scripts in that kind of folder run for desktop sessions. They are not read by the X server as its configuration.

q.q: A colleague suggests running xhost + so a remote program can show its window. What does that command do?
o: It prints the list of hosts that currently hold an open session
Without a plus sign, xhost with no arguments prints the current access list. With the plus sign, it changes it.
It allows only the local machine to connect
That would be a command such as xhost +local:, with a specific name. The bare plus means everybody.
It starts an X server on the remote host
xhost never starts a server. It only edits who may connect to one that is already running.
It disables host access control, so any host may connect
Right. That lets anyone who can reach the display port draw windows and read keystrokes. It is a serious risk.

q.q: User bob uses su to become alice and starts a graphical app. It stops with: Authorization required, but no authorization protocol specified. Which tool manages the cookie that the X server demands?
o: xauth
Right. xauth shows and edits the MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE entries in ~/.Xauthority. Alice's session needs bob's cookie merged in, or xhost to allow her.
xdpyinfo
xdpyinfo prints facts about an X display. It does not manage authorization.
startx
startx launches a new X session. It does not hand cookies to other accounts.
xrandr
xrandr changes the resolution and monitor layout, nothing to do with access cookies.

q.q: After login a user sees only a blank screen, then the desktop closes. Which file is the first place to look for error messages from programs the graphical session started for that user?
o: /etc/X11/xorg.conf
That file holds settings, not messages. Errors go to log files.
~/.bash_logout
That script runs when a login shell ends. It does not record session errors.
~/.xsession-errors
Right. The session writes the error output of the programs it starts into this file in the user's home folder.
/var/spool/cron/crontabs
That folder holds scheduled jobs and is unrelated to graphical login failures.

q.q:
A technician checks a Linux host with ss -tlnp and sees this line:
LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:3389 0.0.0.0:* users:(("xrdp",pid=912,fd=11))
Which remote desktop protocol is the host offering, and what can connect to it from Windows with no extra software?
o: VNC, which needs a viewer installed on Windows
VNC servers normally listen on 5900 and up, not 3389.
RDP, which the built-in Windows Remote Desktop client can use
Right. Port 3389 is the default RDP port, and xrdp is an RDP server for Linux. Windows already includes an RDP client.
XDMCP, which needs an X server on the client
XDMCP uses UDP port 177 and is not what xrdp provides.
Spice, which only works between virtual machines on one hypervisor
Spice is a protocol for virtual machine consoles and does not use port 3389.

q.q: A technician starts a VNC server on a Linux host as display :2. To which TCP port should the viewer connect, using the usual default numbering?
o: 5900 is display :0, the first one. Display :2 is two steps higher.
3389 is the default port of RDP, not VNC.
177 is a UDP port used by XDMCP, which is a different way to reach a remote login screen.
Right. VNC counts up from port 5900, so display :2 uses 5900 + 2 = 5902.

q.q:
A user says quick taps on the keyboard do nothing: a letter appears only when the key is held for about a third of a second. The desktop settings show:
stickykeys-enable   false
slowkeys-enable     true  (delay 300 ms)
bouncekeys-enable   false
togglekeys-enable   true
Which setting causes the problem?
o: stickykeys-enable, which waits for the second key of a shortcut
It is false in the output, and sticky keys only link shortcut keys together.
slowkeys-enable, which ignores a key until it is held long enough
Right. Slow keys accept a key only after the delay, here 300 ms. Turning it off restores normal typing.
bouncekeys-enable, because it is turned off
Bounce keys ignore fast repeats of the same key. Being off cannot delay a first press.
togglekeys-enable, which plays a sound and holds back the key
Toggle keys only beep when Caps Lock or Num Lock changes. They never hold back a key press.

q.q: A user's hands shake, so one key often registers twice within a fraction of a second. Which setting tells the system to ignore a repeat press of the same key that comes too quickly?
o: Sticky keys
Sticky keys help with key combinations, not with double presses.
A screen magnifier
A magnifier enlarges part of the screen for low-vision users. It does not change how key presses are read.
Bounce keys
Right. Bounce keys set a short delay during which a repeated press of the same key is ignored.
High contrast theme
A high contrast theme changes colors for readability and does not affect typing.

q.q: A line in /etc/passwd reads: bob:x:1001:1001:Bob Lee:/home/bob:/bin/bash. What does the x in the second field mean?
o: The password hash is kept in /etc/shadow
Right. The x is a placeholder. Hashes live in /etc/shadow, which only root can read, while /etc/passwd must stay world-readable.
The account is locked and cannot log in
A lock is shown with an exclamation mark at the start of the hash in /etc/shadow, not with an x in /etc/passwd.
The account has no password at all
An empty field would mean that. The x tells programs to look in /etc/shadow for the real value.
The password expired and must be changed
Expiry dates are stored in /etc/shadow, in the aging fields after the hash.

q.q: User bob belongs to the supplementary groups dev and docker. An admin runs: usermod -G wheel bob. What is the result?
o: bob is now in dev, docker and wheel together
That would need the -a option together with -G. Without it the list is replaced.
The command fails because bob is logged in
usermod can change group lists while the user is logged in. The change applies at the next login.
wheel becomes bob's primary group
The primary group is changed with a lowercase -g. A capital -G only sets supplementary groups.
wheel only, plus bob's primary group
Right. -G replaces the whole list of supplementary groups. To add a group and keep the others, use -aG.

q.q: An admin ran usermod -L bob on a default Debian or RHEL server (UsePAM yes). Bob still logs in over SSH with his key pair. Why?
o: Locking only disables the password; key-based login does not use a password
Right. usermod -L puts an exclamation mark in front of the hash in /etc/shadow. To stop all logins, also expire the account (usermod -e 1 bob) or set a nologin shell.
usermod -L was never written to /etc/shadow because bob was logged in
The lock is written to /etc/shadow immediately. The hash gets the exclamation mark.
sshd reads /etc/shadow only for the public key
Key login reads authorized_keys. The lock mark in /etc/shadow only matters to password checks.
Keys always override group membership
Groups are not involved. The lock removes password login and nothing else.

q.q: After userdel carol was run (no options), ls -l in /home/carol shows files owned by the number 1004 instead of a name. What explains this?
o: The filesystem was corrupted by userdel
userdel only edits the account files. It does not damage the filesystem.
Group ownership was removed, so ls shows only the user ID
The numbers show the owner, not the group, and group files are unchanged here.
The home stayed, but no account owns UID 1004 now
Right. Without -r, userdel leaves the home folder and mail spool. Files keep the numeric owner, which now has no name.
The ls command hides names for deleted users on purpose
ls prints a number whenever the lookup of the ID fails. It is not a privacy feature.

q.q: A new employee, alice, must choose a new password the first time she logs in. Which command makes her do that?
o: chage -M 0 alice
-M sets the maximum age in days. A value of 0 would mean the password is always too old, which is not how this is normally done.
chage -d 0 alice
Right. Setting the last-change date to 0 marks the password as expired, so the system asks for a new one at the next login. passwd -e alice does the same.
usermod -p alice alice
-p sets an encrypted password, and here would store a bad hash.
passwd -l alice
-l locks the password, so she could not log in at all.

q.q: A system account has this /etc/shadow entry: svc:*:19700:0:99999:7:::. What does the asterisk in the password field mean?
o: The password is the single character *
The field holds a hash, never plain text. The asterisk is not hashed to anything.
The password is expired and the user must change it
Expiry is controlled by the date fields after the hash.
The account has an empty password
An empty field would allow a login with no password. The asterisk is the opposite.
No hash can match, so password login is impossible
Right. A value that cannot be a valid hash blocks password authentication. It is common for service accounts.

q.q: Alice's account comes from a central LDAP server. grep alice /etc/passwd shows nothing, yet she logs in fine. Which command shows her account entry the way the system sees it?
o: cat /etc/shadow | grep alice
That shows the local shadow file only, and it would be empty for a remote account too.
id -un alice
id -un alice prints only the user name. It does not show the account entry.
getent passwd alice
Right. getent asks the Name Service Switch, so it searches local files and every configured source such as LDAP.
passwd -S alice
That shows password status, not the account entry. For remote accounts it may fail too.

q.q: Which file holds the default PASS_MAX_DAYS and the UID range that useradd uses for new accounts?
o: /etc/passwd
That file lists existing accounts. It stores no defaults for new ones.
/etc/login.defs
Right. login.defs sets site-wide defaults such as password aging and UID_MIN. /etc/default/useradd holds a few more, like the default shell.
/etc/skel/.profile
That file is only a template copied into new home folders.
/etc/group
That file lists groups and their members, not account defaults.

q.q: An admin must move bob's home folder to /srv/bob and keep his files. Which command does both steps?
o: usermod -d /srv/bob -m bob
Right. -d sets the new home path, and -m moves the old folder's contents to it.
usermod -d /srv/bob bob
Without -m the record changes, but the files stay in the old place.
usermod -m /srv/bob bob
-m has no path. It only works together with -d.
useradd -d /srv/bob bob
useradd is for new accounts and would fail because bob already exists.

q.q: Which command creates user dana with a home folder, the existing group audit as her primary group, and wheel as an additional group?
o: useradd -m -g wheel -G audit dana
This swaps the two options, so wheel becomes primary and audit becomes the extra group.
useradd -m -g audit -G wheel dana
Right. Lowercase -g names the primary group. Capital -G names the supplementary groups.
useradd -m -g audit,wheel dana
-g accepts exactly one group. A list must be given with -G.
useradd -m -p audit -G wheel dana
-p sets the password hash, so the word audit would be stored as a password value.

q.q: Which statement is true for this crontab line? 0 3 1 * 1 /usr/local/bin/report.sh
o: At 03:00 on the 1st and also at 03:00 every Monday
Right. When both the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are restricted, cron runs the job if either one matches.
It runs at 03:00 only when the first of the month is a Monday
That would be an AND rule, which cron does not use for these two fields.
It runs at 03:00 every day, because the fields cancel out
Neither field is a star, so the line is restricted by both.
It runs at 01:00 on every third day
The first field is minutes and the second is hours, so 0 3 means 03:00.

q.q: An admin drops the file /etc/cron.d/sync with this content: */15 * * * * /usr/local/bin/sync.sh. The job never runs and the cron log complains about a bad username. What is wrong?
o: Cron.d files must end in .cron
Cron reads regular files in that folder. The name does not need a special ending.
The */15 syntax is not allowed in cron.d
Step values are valid in any crontab format.
They need a user name before the command
Right. System cron files have six fields before the command: five time fields, then the user name.
The script must first be added with crontab -e
crontab -e edits a user's own table. Files in /etc/cron.d are read directly.

q.q: Bob runs crontab -e and gets: You (bob) are not allowed to use this program. The file /etc/cron.allow exists. What is the cause?
o: bob is listed in /etc/cron.deny only
If cron.allow exists, cron.deny is not even checked.
Only root may ever use crontab
Normal users can have a crontab unless a policy file blocks them.
The /var/spool/cron folder is still empty for bob
An empty spool just means no jobs yet. It does not stop a user from adding one.
bob is not listed in /etc/cron.allow
Right. When cron.allow exists, only the users named in it may use crontab. cron.deny is then ignored.

q.q: A crontab line reads: @reboot /usr/local/bin/start-agent.sh. When does cron run it?
o: Every time any user logs in over SSH
Logins do not trigger cron. Login scripts belong in the shell startup files.
Once at the next reboot only, then the line is removed
cron never edits the table. The line runs after every start of the daemon.
Once each time the cron daemon starts, such as after a boot
Right. @reboot is a special time word. It runs the job at startup of cron, not on a schedule.
Every minute until the machine is rebooted
Per-minute jobs use five stars. @reboot has no repeat interval.

q.q: An at job was queued by mistake and atq shows it as number 12. Which command removes it?
o: at -d 13
-d is accepted on some systems, but 13 is the wrong job here, so it removes someone else's job.
crontab -r 12
crontab -r removes your whole crontab and does not take a job number.
killall at
Queued jobs are not running processes. There is nothing to kill.
atrm 12
Right. atrm deletes the queued job with that number, and atq confirms the queue is clean.

q.q: On a server there is no /etc/at.allow and no /etc/at.deny file. Who may use the at command?
o: Every user
That is the result of an empty /etc/at.deny file, not of having no files at all.
Only the superuser
Right. If neither file exists, at is limited to root. An empty at.deny, by contrast, allows everyone.
Nobody, not even root
Root is always allowed to use at.
Only users in group at
No such group rule exists in the standard at configuration.

q.q: An admin wrote backup.service and backup.timer (with OnCalendar=daily) in /etc/systemd/system and ran systemctl daemon-reload. Nothing is scheduled yet. Which command starts the schedule now and keeps it after reboots?
o: systemctl enable --now backup.timer
Right. The timer unit triggers the service. Enabling it makes it start at boot, and --now starts it immediately.
systemctl enable --now backup.service
That would start the job once and enable it at boot, but would not create a schedule.
systemctl start backup.service
This runs the backup a single time. Nothing is scheduled.
systemctl daemon-reload backup.timer
daemon-reload takes no unit name and only rereads unit files.

q.q: Without writing unit files, an admin needs /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh to run once, 30 minutes from now, under systemd. Which command does that?
o: systemd-run --on-active=30m /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh
Right. systemd-run creates a transient timer and service. The job runs once after the delay and then the units disappear.
systemctl enable --on-active=30m cleanup.sh
systemctl enable has no timer option and takes a unit name, not a script path.
at systemd 30m cleanup.sh
at needs a time and reads commands from input, so this line is not valid.
systemd-timer --delay 30 cleanup.sh
There is no command by that name.

q.q: What does this crontab schedule mean? */10 9-17 * * 1-5
o: Every 10 hours between 9 and 17, on Monday through Friday
The first field is minutes. It steps in minutes, not hours.
Every 10 minutes from 09:00 through 17:00, every day
The last field limits it to weekdays, and the 17:00 hour runs until 17:50.
Every 10 minutes, 09:00 to 17:50, Monday to Friday
Right. The hour range 9-17 includes the whole 17:00 hour, so the last run is at 17:50.
Once at 09:10 and once at 17:10 on weekdays
A step value repeats many times within a range, so there are far more runs.

q.q: An admin runs timedatectl set-timezone Europe/Berlin. What does this change on a typical systemd system?
o: It rewrites the hardware clock to Berlin time
The hardware clock is set separately, and it usually stays in UTC.
It edits the TZ variable in /etc/profile
The system zone does not use /etc/profile. TZ is only an override.
It restarts the cron daemon so jobs use the new zone
The change is applied through /etc/localtime. No restart is needed.
It relinks /etc/localtime to the Europe/Berlin zone file
Right. The zone is a link to a compiled zoneinfo file. The system clock itself (UTC) does not change, only how it is shown.

q.q: A user wants to see what time it is in Tokyo for one command only, without changing any system setting. Which line does that?
o: export LC_TIME=Asia/Tokyo; date
LC_TIME controls the format of dates, not the zone, and Asia/Tokyo is not a valid locale name.
TZ=Asia/Tokyo date
Right. A variable set in front of a command lasts only for that command. The date command uses TZ to pick the zone.
timedatectl set-timezone Asia/Tokyo
That changes the zone for the whole system, which is not wanted here.
date --tz Tokyo
date has no --tz option.

q.q: A shell has these variables: LANG=de_DE.UTF-8, LC_MESSAGES=fr_FR.UTF-8 and LC_ALL=C. Which locale does a command like sort use for collation?
o: C
Right. LC_ALL overrides every LC_* category and also LANG, so all categories use C.
de_DE.UTF-8
LANG is only the fallback, and LC_ALL beats it.
fr_FR.UTF-8
LC_MESSAGES only affects message language, not sorting, and LC_ALL beats it anyway.
A mix of all three, chosen per word
Each category uses one locale, never a mix per word.

q.q: A legacy file report.txt is encoded in ISO-8859-1. Which command writes a UTF-8 copy named report-utf8.txt?
o: iconv -f UTF-8 -t ISO-8859-1 report.txt -o report-utf8.txt
The source and target are swapped, which would try to read UTF-8 as ISO-8859-1.
iconv -l ISO-8859-1 report.txt
-l only lists the encodings iconv knows.
iconv -f ISO-8859-1 -t UTF-8 report.txt -o report-utf8.txt
Right. -f names the source encoding and -t names the target. -o names the output file.
locale -c UTF-8 < report.txt > report-utf8.txt
locale shows environment settings and has no -c conversion option.

q.q: Which command lists the locales that are installed and usable on the system?
o: locale
With no options it shows the current variables such as LANG, not the list of installed ones.
localedef --list
localedef builds locale definitions. Its listing option differs and it is not the standard way to list them.
tzselect -a
tzselect picks time zones and has nothing to do with locales.
locale -a
Right. locale -a prints every locale installed. Plain locale shows only the settings of your current environment.

q.q: A text file shows as: cafÃ© instead of café. Which explanation fits best?
o: The file is stored in ASCII
ASCII has no accented letters at all, and a real ASCII file would not contain them.
UTF-8 bytes shown as ISO-8859-1
Right. In UTF-8 the letter é uses two bytes. A viewer that reads each byte as a Latin-1 character shows Ã and ©.
The file is corrupted and the data is lost
The data is fine. Using the right encoding in the viewer restores the text.
The terminal font is too small to show accents
A small font would make text hard to read, not change the characters.

q.q: What does the tzselect command do?
o: It changes /etc/localtime for the whole system
tzselect does not modify system files. It only helps you find the name.
It lists the hardware clock settings
The hardware clock is handled by hwclock.
It asks where you are and prints a TZ value
Right. tzselect only prints a value to use. You still have to put it in your profile or set it with timedatectl.
It converts text files between two character sets
That is iconv's job.

q.q: An auditor asks for the password-aging settings of the account alice, such as the maximum age and warning days. Which TWO commands show them? (Choose two.)
o: getent group alice
That prints the group entry and has no aging data.
chage -l alice
Right. chage -l lists the last change, the expiry date, and the minimum, maximum and warning values.
grep alice /etc/passwd
The passwd file holds no aging fields. They are in /etc/shadow.
passwd -S alice
Right. -S prints a one-line status for the account that includes the minimum, maximum, warning and inactivity values.
id alice
id shows the numeric IDs and the groups, not password aging.

q.q: An admin tries timedatectl set-time '2026-11-27 09:00:00' and gets: Failed to set time: Automatic time synchronization is enabled. What should be done first, if the time truly has to be set by hand?
o: Run timedatectl set-ntp false
Right. While NTP sync is on, the service owns the clock and refuses manual changes. Turning it off allows set-time.
Run hwclock --hctosys
That copies the hardware clock into the system clock. It does not switch off synchronization.
Delete /etc/localtime
That file holds the time zone, which has nothing to do with sync being on.
Reboot into rescue mode
Rescue mode is not needed. The message tells which setting is blocking the change.

q.q: The system clock was corrected by NTP, but the hardware clock still has the old time. Which command copies the system time to the hardware clock?
o: hwclock --hctosys
This copies the hardware clock into the system clock, which would put the wrong time back.
hwclock --show
--show only displays the hardware clock.
date --set=hardware
date does not write to the hardware clock, and this is not a valid option.
hwclock --systohc
Right. systohc means system to hardware clock. The reverse direction is --hctosys.

q.q: In the output of chronyc sources, which marker at the start of a line shows the server the system clock is currently synchronized to?
o: A plus marks a good candidate that is combined or kept in reserve, not the chosen source.
Right. The caret means a server, and the asterisk marks the one chosen as the current time source.
A minus marks a source that is not combined with the selected one.
A question mark means the source's reachability is lost or it has not yet been tested.

q.q: What is the purpose of the name pool.ntp.org in an NTP configuration?
o: It is the one atomic clock that every Linux system must use
The pool is a cluster of many servers run by volunteers, not a single clock.
A DNS name that returns many volunteer time servers
Right. Using the pool spreads load. Each lookup returns different servers from a large group.
It is a local file that keeps the list of leap seconds
Leap seconds are announced by time servers and not stored in a file called this.
It is a license server for chrony
chrony is free software and needs no license check.

q.q: A line in /etc/chrony.conf reads: pool 2.pool.ntp.org iburst. What does the iburst option add?
o: It sends a quick burst of packets so sync starts faster
Right. Without it, the first sync can take a few minutes. iburst speeds up the first few exchanges.
It forces the server to answer only over IPv6
The IP version is not decided by iburst.
It makes chrony step the clock backward at every single poll
Stepping is controlled by makestep, not iburst.
It blocks the pool unless the system clock is already correct
iburst does not test the system clock. It only changes the early polling.

q.q: An admin wants to know how far a server's clock is off from pool.ntp.org, without changing the clock. Which command asks the server and only prints the offset?
o: ntpdate -b pool.ntp.org
Without -q, ntpdate sets the clock, and -b even forces it to step the time.
hwclock --adjust
--adjust corrects the hardware clock for drift and does not query a time server.
date -s pool.ntp.org --utc
date -s sets the time from a date string and would reject this name.
ntpdate -q pool.ntp.org
Right. -q means query only, so the command reports the offset and leaves the clock alone.

q.q: A PC dual-boots Windows and Linux. After booting Linux, its clock is off by exactly the local UTC offset. What is the usual cause?
o: The ntpd service has crashed and is no longer correcting the time
A crashed sync service would cause slow drift, not a jump of exactly the zone offset.
The kernel does not support time zones
Linux handles zones fine. The question is about what the hardware clock holds.
Windows stores local time in the clock; Linux assumes UTC
Right. Both systems read the same chip but disagree about its meaning. Set Windows to UTC, or tell Linux with timedatectl set-local-rtc 1.
The BIOS battery is dead, so the clock resets to a wrong time
A dead battery would reset the clock to a very old date, not an exact zone offset.

q.q: A line in /etc/rsyslog.conf reads: *.info;mail.none;authpriv.none /var/log/messages. What does mail.none do?
o: It writes only mail messages to the file
That would be mail.* alone. Here none removes mail messages.
It leaves mail facility messages out of this file
Right. none means that facility is excluded from the rule. Mail logs have their own file.
It disables the mail service
A log rule only filters messages. It never starts or stops a service.
It sends mail messages to the root user
Sending to a user needs a user name as the destination, not a selector word.

q.q: Which command sends a test message to the syslog facility local4 with priority err, labelled with the tag deploy?
o: logger -f local4 -l err "test message"
These are not logger options. -f means read from a file.
syslog local4.err deploy "test message"
There is no command with this form.
echo local4.err > /dev/log
Writing plain text this way does not create a properly formed syslog message.
logger -p local4.err -t deploy "test message"
Right. -p takes facility.priority and -t sets the tag shown in the log line.

q.q: An rsyslog selector is written *.err. Which messages does it match?
o: err and every more severe level: crit, alert and emerg
Right. A priority in a selector includes all levels above it, unless an equals sign is used.
Only err messages
Only an equals form such as *.=err does that.
err and the less severe levels warning, notice and info
Severity goes the other way. A lower level is not included.
Every message from every facility
That is *.debug, since debug is the lowest priority.

q.q: A systemd server just booted after a crash. Which command shows only messages of priority error or worse from the current boot?
o: journalctl -k
-k shows kernel messages only, of every priority.
journalctl -b -1
-b -1 is the previous boot, with all priorities.
journalctl -p err -b
Right. -p filters by priority (including worse ones) and -b limits to the current boot.
journalctl --disk-usage
This prints how much space the journal uses and shows no messages.

q.q: After a reboot, journalctl -b -1 reports that no persistent journal was found, so the previous boot's logs are gone. Which fix makes logs survive reboots?
o: Run journalctl --rotate every night to keep older boots
Rotation makes new files. It does not move the journal out of /run.
Create /var/log/journal, then restart systemd-journald
Right. Without that folder the journal is kept in /run, which is erased at shutdown.
Set Storage=volatile in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and restart
Volatile means memory only, which is the cause of the problem.
Install rsyslog and then remove systemd-journald from the system
systemd-journald cannot be removed, and rsyslog does not change journal storage.

q.q: A logrotate stanza for /var/log/app/*.log contains: weekly, rotate 4, compress. Which result does it give?
o: Weekly rotation, keeping four old copies
Right. rotate 4 keeps four rotated files. Compress shrinks the older ones.
Logs are rotated four times a week
weekly is the interval, once a week. The 4 is the number of copies kept.
Logs are deleted every four weeks without any copy
Old copies are kept up to four, not deleted at once.
Logs older than four days are compressed and the rest is deleted
The rule is based on the count of rotated files, not on the age in days.

q.q: After logrotate runs, app.log.1 grows and the new app.log stays empty. The daemon keeps writing to the renamed file. Which logrotate option makes it write to the fresh file without restarting the daemon?
o: missingok
That only stops errors when a log file does not exist.
notifempty
That skips rotation of empty files, which does not affect where the daemon writes.
dateext
That adds a date to rotated file names and has no effect on the open file.
copytruncate
Right. It copies the log and then empties the original file, so the daemon keeps using the same open file.

q.q: On a Red Hat family server without Debian-style logs, where would you look first for failed SSH logins in the traditional log files?
o: /var/log/auth.log
That file name is used on Debian and Ubuntu, not on Red Hat family systems.
/var/log/dmesg
That file holds early kernel messages from boot, not logins.
/var/log/secure
Right. RHEL-based systems record authentication messages in /var/log/secure. Debian-based ones use /var/log/auth.log.
/var/log/lastlog
That is a binary file read with the lastlog command. It holds last login times, not failed attempts.

q.q: A user wants every message sent to her account on the server to be passed on to alice@example.com. She has no root rights. Where does she set this?
o: In /etc/aliases, with newaliases
That needs root and applies to the whole system.
In the file ~/.forward in her home folder
Right. MTAs read ~/.forward for the user's own forwarding address. No root access is needed.
In ~/.mailrc with a forward keyword
~/.mailrc configures the mail command, not the delivery of incoming mail.
In /var/spool/mail/alice
That is where her mailbox messages are stored, not a configuration file.

q.q: An admin adds the line support: bob, carol to /etc/aliases, but mail to support still bounces as unknown user. What is the missing step?
o: Run postqueue -f to flush the whole mail queue now
A flush resends queued mail. The alias map itself is still the old one.
Remove the space after the colon
A space after the colon is normal in an aliases file.
Run newaliases to rebuild the alias map
Right. MTAs read a compiled copy of the aliases file. The edit takes effect after newaliases (or postalias).
Reboot the server
A reboot is not required. Rebuilding the database is enough.

q.q: Users say that mail is not arriving. Which command lists the messages that are waiting in the local queue, with their IDs and reasons for delay?
o: mailq
Right. mailq prints the queue, usually the same data as postqueue -p on Postfix.
mail -q
The mail command is for reading and sending, and -q is not a queue listing.
newaliases
That rebuilds the alias database and shows no queue.
lpq
lpq shows print jobs, not mail.

q.q: A monitoring script calls /usr/sbin/sendmail -t to send alerts. The server runs Postfix and no Sendmail package. Why does the script still work?
o: Linux creates a sendmail link for every network card
Nothing like that exists. The command comes from the MTA package.
The kernel forwards sendmail calls to cron
cron is a scheduler and has no part in mail delivery.
The script automatically installs Sendmail on first run
Scripts do not install packages by themselves, and the path is already provided.
Postfix provides a sendmail command at that path
Right. MTAs such as Postfix and Exim provide an emulation layer so old scripts keep working.

q.q: Which command sends the contents of /var/log/backup.log to ops@example.com with the subject Backup failed?
o: mail -f "Backup failed" ops@example.com < /var/log/backup.log
-f means read a mailbox file, not subject text.
mail -s "Backup failed" ops@example.com < /var/log/backup.log
Right. -s sets the subject and the redirect supplies the body from the file.
mailq -s "Backup failed" ops@example.com
mailq lists the queue and sends nothing.
newaliases ops@example.com < /var/log/backup.log
newaliases only rebuilds the alias database and ignores its input.

q.q:
On a Postfix server, mailq prints:
-Queue ID-  --Size-- ----Arrival Time---- -Sender/Recipient-------
3F2A41B02C*    1520 Fri Nov 27 09:12:44  alice@app01.example.com
                                          bob@example.org
7B91D2A1E0     3402 Fri Nov 27 08:01:10  root@app01.example.com
(connect to mail.example.org[203.0.113.25]:25: Connection timed out)
                                          ops@example.org
What is the state of message 7B91D2A1E0?
o: Bounced: the sender has already received a failure notice
A bounce removes the message from the queue and sends a report. This one is still waiting.
Delivered: it is listed only until the log is rotated
Delivered mail leaves the queue. A message with a connection error was not delivered.
Deferred: the remote server did not answer, and Postfix will try again later
Right. The text in parentheses is the reason for the delay. Postfix keeps deferred mail in the queue and retries it.
Active: it is being delivered right now, as the asterisk shows
The asterisk is on 3F2A41B02C, not on this message, and it marks an active message.

q.q:
Users say jobs sent to printer hp1 are accepted but nothing prints. These commands show:
$ lpstat -a
hp1 accepting requests since Fri 27 Nov 2026 08:00:12
$ lpstat -p hp1
printer hp1 disabled since Fri 27 Nov 2026 09:03:11 - Paused
Which command gets printing going again?
o: cupsaccept hp1, so the queue starts taking jobs
lpstat -a already says hp1 is accepting requests.
lprm -P hp1 -, to clear the stuck jobs first
That deletes the waiting jobs and still leaves the printer disabled.
cupsreject hp1, to stop the queue from filling up
That would make the queue refuse new jobs and does not restart printing.
cupsenable hp1, which resumes the paused printer
Right. The queue accepts jobs, but the printer itself is disabled. cupsenable lets it print what is waiting.

q.q: Where does CUPS keep the definitions of the print queues that were added on the server?
o: /etc/cups/printers.conf
Right. This file lists each queue with its device URI. cupsd.conf in the same folder configures the daemon itself.
/etc/cups/cupsd.conf
That file configures the daemon, such as the listening port and access rules.
/var/spool/cups/printers.list
The spool folder holds waiting jobs. There is no such queue list there.
/etc/printcap.d/queues
A printcap file is used by the old LPD system and is not where CUPS stores queues.

q.q: Job 42 on the queue hp1 was sent by mistake. Which command removes it from the queue?
o: lpr -P hp1 -r 42
lpr -r removes the file after it is printed. It does not delete jobs.
cupsreject hp1
That stops the queue from accepting new jobs. It does not remove job 42.
lpq -P hp1 -d 42
lpq only lists jobs and takes no delete option.
lprm -P hp1 42
Right. lprm removes a job by number from a queue. cancel 42 does the same in CUPS.

q.q: Which command prints two copies of report.pdf on the queue hp1 with the lpd-style tool?
o: lpr -d hp1 -n 2 report.pdf
-d and -n belong to the lp command, and lpr would not understand them this way.
lpr -P hp1 -#2 report.pdf
Right. lpr selects the queue with -P and the number of copies with -#.
lpq -P hp1 -#2 report.pdf
lpq lists jobs and does not print.
lprm -P hp1 -#2 report.pdf
lprm removes jobs and does not print files.

q.q: The printer hp1 needs a paper-jam repair. You want users to keep sending jobs to its queue, but nothing should print until it is fixed. Which command does that?
o: cupsdisable hp1
Right. A disabled printer still accepts jobs into the queue. They wait until you run cupsenable.
cupsreject -r "paper jam" hp1
A rejected queue refuses new jobs with an error, so users lose their prints.
lprm -P hp1 -
That removes all pending jobs, which is not wanted.
cupsaccept hp1
That makes the queue take new jobs. It does not stop printing.

q.q: A backup script must put a status line into the system log so it appears in journalctl. Which TWO commands do that? (Choose two.)
o: logger -t backup "nightly run finished"
Right. logger sends the text to the syslog socket, which systemd-journald reads, so it shows up in journalctl.
journalctl --append "nightly run finished"
journalctl is for reading the journal. It has no option to add entries.
echo "nightly run finished" > /var/log/journal/backup
The journal is stored in a binary format. A plain write to that folder is not a valid entry.
echo "nightly run finished" | systemd-cat -t backup
Right. systemd-cat connects the output of a command to the journal and -t sets the identifier.
tail -f /var/log/messages
That follows a file on screen and writes nothing to the log.

q.q: A host has the address 192.168.10.77/26. What is the network address of its subnet?
o: That would be the network for a /24. With a /26 the first block ends at .63.
Network addresses of a /26 are multiples of 64, and 76 is not one.
Right. A /26 uses blocks of 64 addresses: .0, .64, .128 and .192. The address .77 falls in the block that starts at .64.
That block starts above .77, so the address is not in it.

q.q:
A host prints this routing table:
default via 10.0.5.1 dev eth0
10.0.5.0/27 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.5.20
It now sends a packet to 10.0.5.45. What happens?
o: It goes to the default gateway 10.0.5.1, because .45 is outside 10.0.5.0/27
Right. A /27 covers 10.0.5.0 to 10.0.5.31. The address .45 is in the next block, so it is not on the local link.
It is sent straight to 10.0.5.45 on the local link, since it starts with 10.0.5
Only the mask matters. With /27 the host part is just the last 5 bits.
It is dropped, because no route lists 10.0.5.45 by name
The default route matches every address that no other route covers.
It is sent to 10.0.5.31, the broadcast address of the subnet
The packet's destination stays .45. A broadcast address is not used as a next hop.

q.q:
ip -br addr prints:
lo       UNKNOWN  127.0.0.1/8
eth0     UP       172.31.8.14/20
eth1     UP       198.51.100.77/24
docker0  DOWN     172.17.0.1/16
For this exercise treat 198.51.100.0/24 as an ordinary public range. Which interface has a public address?
o: 172.16.0.0/12 runs through 172.31.255.255, so this address is private.
172.17.x.x is also inside 172.16.0.0/12, so it is private.
127.0.0.0/8 is the loopback range and never leaves the host.
Right. It is outside the loopback and the private ranges, so it can be routed on the internet.

q.q: A laptop on the office network shows the address 169.254.33.8. What does that most likely mean?
o: It was handed out as a public address by the ISP's router to the office
169.254.0.0/16 is reserved for link-local use and is never handed out as a public address.
It asked for a DHCP address, got none, and chose one itself
Right. Addresses in 169.254.0.0/16 are self-assigned when DHCP is not available. They only work on the local link.
It is the address of the default gateway on the office network
A gateway has an address inside the real subnet, not a self-assigned one.
It is an IPv6 address written in short form
Dotted numbers are IPv4. IPv6 uses colons.

q.q: Which statement about ICMP is correct?
o: It uses TCP port 7 for every ping
Ping does not use TCP or any port number.
It is a transport protocol like UDP that carries file transfers
ICMP reports errors and status. It does not move user data.
Control messages such as echo requests, with no port numbers
Right. ICMP rides directly on IP and uses message types and codes. Ping uses echo request and echo reply.
It is used by DNS to send large answers
DNS uses UDP, and TCP for large answers. ICMP is not involved.

q.q: An interface shows the IPv6 address fe80::a00:27ff:fe4e:66a1. What kind of address is it?
o: A global unicast address that works on the internet
Global addresses today start with 2000::/3, such as 2001: or 2a00:.
The loopback address of the host
Loopback is ::1 only.
A multicast address
Multicast addresses start with ff.
Link-local, valid only on the local network segment
Right. fe80::/10 is the link-local range. Every IPv6 interface gets one, and routers never forward it.

q.q: Which is a valid shortened form of the IPv6 address 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?
o: The double colon can appear only once in an address.
This leaves out the information needed to rebuild the address. It has too few groups and no double colon.
Right. Leading zeros can be dropped in each group, and one run of all-zero groups can be replaced by a double colon.
This uses two double colons, which is not allowed.

q.q: A PC has the address 10.0.5.20/24 and wants to reach 10.0.6.30. What does it need in order to send the packet?
o: A default gateway on its own subnet, because the destination is on another network
Right. 10.0.6.30 is outside 10.0.5.0/24, so the PC hands the packet to a router.
Nothing, since both addresses start with 10.0
Only the network part set by the mask matters. With a /24 the third number differs, so they are different networks.
A second IP address in the 10.0.6.0 range
A single address and a route to a router are enough. A second address is not required.
A DNS server entry, because the destination is a name
DNS maps names to addresses. The question is about routing, not about names.

q.q: Which file maps service names, such as smtp or https, to port numbers and protocols for local tools?
o: /etc/protocols
That file maps protocol names like tcp and icmp to IP protocol numbers, not to service ports.
/etc/services
Right. Programs such as netstat and getent use it to show names instead of numbers.
/etc/hosts
That file maps host names to IP addresses.
/etc/inetd.conf
That file configures a super server and its services. It is not the name-to-port table.

q.q: On a system managed by NetworkManager, which sequence gives the connection named Wired a static address that survives reboots?
o: ip addr add 192.168.1.50/24 dev eth0 followed by ip link set eth0 up
This works at once, but the change is lost at reboot.
echo 192.168.1.50/24 > /etc/hostname, then restart NetworkManager
/etc/hostname holds the host name, not an address.
ifconfig eth0 192.168.1.50 up, placed in /etc/rc.local at boot
That is a hand-made workaround, and NetworkManager would still manage the interface and may override it.
nmcli con mod Wired ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.50/24, then nmcli con up Wired
Right. The profile is saved to disk. The connection is brought up again so the new values take effect.

q.q: An admin ran hostname web07 and the new name shows at once. After a reboot the old name returns. Which command changes it permanently?
o: hostname -f web07
-f prints the fully qualified name. It does not save anything.
hostnamectl set-hostname web07
Right. This writes the static name to /etc/hostname and also updates the running name.
echo web07 > /etc/hosts
That would overwrite the hosts file and break local name lookups.
nmcli general reload hostname web07
The word web07 is not an argument of that command, and it would not save a host name.

q.q: A server's /etc/hosts holds 10.1.1.9 db01, but DNS was updated and now says db01 is 10.1.1.40. Applications still connect to the old address. Which setting explains this?
o: files before dns in /etc/nsswitch.conf, so /etc/hosts wins
Right. NSS tries sources in the order listed. The first source with an answer wins, so the old line in /etc/hosts is used.
The nameserver line in /etc/resolv.conf points to an old server
DNS is not even being asked here, since the local file answers first.
The DNS cache on the server is too small
The answer comes from the local file and not from a cache.
The hosts file is read only at boot
It is read each time a name is looked up.

q.q: An admin edits /etc/resolv.conf on a NetworkManager system. After the next reboot the edit is gone. What is the proper way to set DNS servers that stay?
o: chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf so that NetworkManager cannot rewrite it
+i makes the file immutable. It would keep the old server and block NetworkManager from updating it.
Add the DNS server to /etc/hosts
/etc/hosts maps names to addresses. It is not a list of resolvers.
nmcli con mod <name> ipv4.dns 10.0.0.2, then reactivate
Right. NetworkManager generates resolv.conf from the connection profile, so the setting must go into the profile.
Set the DNS server in /etc/hostname next to the host name
That file holds only the host name.

q.q: On a Debian system that uses /etc/network/interfaces, which line makes eth0 come up automatically at boot?
o: auto eth0
Right. auto tells ifup -a, run at boot, to bring the interface up.
start eth0
start is not a keyword in this file.
ifup eth0 at boot
That is a command you type, not a configuration line.
iface eth0 enabled
iface defines how to configure an interface and expects a method such as dhcp or static, not enabled.

q.q: Which command shows each network device and whether NetworkManager reports it as connected or disconnected?
o: nmcli connection reload
This rereads connection files from disk and prints nothing about device state.
nmcli device status
Right. It lists every device with its type, state and the connection it uses.
nmcli general hostname
This prints or sets the host name.
nmcli radio all
This shows the state of wireless radios only.

q.q: An admin edited a connection file by hand under /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/. NetworkManager does not apply the change. Which step is missing?
o: hostnamectl reload
hostnamectl manages host names and has no reload for connections.
ifdown lo and then ifup lo to restart the loopback interface
The loopback interface is unrelated to the edited profile.
nmcli con reload, then nmcli con up <profile>
Right. NetworkManager must reread the files first. A reload by itself does not reconnect, so bring the profile up too.
systemctl mask NetworkManager
Masking prevents the service from starting at all.

q.q: A temporary default route is needed right now on a server, and it must not survive a reboot. Which command adds it with the modern tool?
o: route -n add default 192.168.1.1
The legacy route command is not valid with these options, and it is not the modern tool.
nmcli con mod Wired ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1
That changes the saved profile, so it would last across reboots.
ip addr add default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0
ip addr manages addresses on interfaces. Routes are under ip route.
ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
Right. ip route changes the running routing table only. A persistent route has to be written in the network profile.

q.q: Which command shows which process is listening on TCP port 8080 and does not try to resolve names?
o: ss -ulnp | grep :8080
-u asks for UDP sockets, which is the wrong protocol for the question.
ip route | grep 8080
ip route shows routes, with no ports.
ss -tlnp | grep :8080
Right. -t is TCP, -l is listening, -n skips name lookups and -p shows the process.
ping -p 8080 localhost
-p in ping sets a data pattern in the packet. It does not test a port.

q.q: A traceroute shows hop 5 as * * * but hops 6, 7 and 8 answer normally and the destination is reached. What does this tell you?
o: Hop 5 drops the probe replies, but traffic still passes through
Right. Many routers and firewalls drop the TTL-exceeded replies. Since later hops respond, the path is fine.
The path is broken at hop 5, so traffic cannot get through
If it were broken, no later hop and no destination would answer.
The destination is blocking ICMP
The destination answered, so ICMP is not blocked there.
DNS failed on hop 5
traceroute prints addresses and tries name lookups for the hops it sees. A lookup failure does not show * * *.

q.q: From a workstation, ping 8.8.8.8 works, but ping example.com says: Temporary failure in name resolution. What should be checked next?
o: The speed and duplex settings of the network card and its cable
The link already carries traffic to an outside address, so the card is working.
The default gateway address
The gateway must be fine because packets reached 8.8.8.8.
The MTU of the first router
An MTU problem causes odd failures with large packets, not a name resolution message.
The DNS settings: resolv.conf and nsswitch.conf order
Right. Reaching an IP address proves routing and the link work. Only the name lookup fails.

q.q: A user cannot reach the default gateway 192.168.1.1. Which command shows whether the gateway's hardware address has been learned on the local link?
o: ip route show
This lists the routes, not the learned hardware addresses.
ip neigh show
Right. The neighbor table holds learned ARP entries. A gateway with state FAILED or INCOMPLETE did not answer.
hostname -I
This prints the host's own addresses.
tracepath 192.168.1.1
tracepath shows the path to a target. It does not display the ARP table.

q.q: Which command tests, without sending data, whether TCP port 5432 on db01 accepts connections?
o: -l makes nc listen on that port on this machine.
nc -zv db01 5432
Right. -z checks the port without sending data and -v prints the result.
nc -u db01 5432
-u uses UDP, which is the wrong protocol for a TCP service.
ping -p 5432 db01
ping has no port test. -p is a data pattern.

q.q: Which tool shows the path to a host and the discovered path MTU, and works for a normal user without root?
o: traceroute -I
-I uses ICMP echo probes and normally needs root.
ping -c 4
ping checks the reachability of one target and does not list hops.
netstat -r
netstat -r prints the routing table. It does not probe the path.
tracepath
Right. tracepath uses ordinary UDP probes, so root is not needed, and it prints the MTU it finds.

q.q: A technician runs ping6 fe80::1 on a server with two interfaces and gets: Invalid argument. What is missing?
o: A scope: fe80::1%eth0, so it knows which link to use
Right. A link-local address is valid on every link, so the interface must be named.
A route to the internet through the default gateway of the server
Link-local addresses do not go through routers. A default route does not help.
A DNS record for the address
The error is about the address, and DNS is not involved.
Root privileges
Ping does not need root for ICMP echo on normal systems.

q.q: An admin must ask the DNS server 10.0.0.2 directly, ignoring what resolv.conf says, for the address of www.example.com. Which command does that?
o: dig www.example.com -s 10.0.0.2
-s is not the option for choosing a server.
host 10.0.0.2 www.example.com
That would look up the name 10.0.0.2 on the server www.example.com, which is backward.
dig @10.0.0.2 www.example.com
Right. The @ sign names the server to ask. Without it, dig uses the servers in resolv.conf.
getent hosts 10.0.0.2 www.example.com
getent follows nsswitch.conf and has no way to pick a DNS server.

q.q: Which command lists the mail servers (MX records) for example.com?
o: host -m example.com
-m is not the option to ask for MX records.
getent mx example.com
getent reads sources set in nsswitch.conf, such as hosts, and has no MX database.
nslookup -mail example.com
The option -mail does not exist. Use set type=mx or -type=mx.
host -t MX example.com
Right. -t picks the record type. dig example.com MX gives the same data.

q.q: A name in /etc/hosts works with ping, but dig for the same name answers NXDOMAIN. Why?
o: The /etc/hosts file is wrong
If the file were wrong, ping would not work either.
dig asks DNS only; ping also reads /etc/hosts
Right. To test what applications see, use getent hosts name. To test DNS itself, use dig.
dig works only with IPv6
dig supports A and AAAA records.
dig cannot read /etc/hosts because it needs root for that
/etc/hosts is readable by everyone. dig simply asks DNS only, by design, and never reads that file.

q.q: A host has /etc/resolv.conf with: search corp.example.com. The user types ping files. Which name does the resolver try first?
o: files.corp.example.com
Right. The search line adds the domain to short names. Names without a dot are tried with each search suffix.
files.com
The resolver adds only the domain listed in the search line.
corp.example.com.files
The suffix goes after the short name, not before it.
It tries only /etc/hosts and gives up
The hosts file is checked first if nsswitch.conf says files. DNS is tried afterwards with the search domain.

q.q: On an Ubuntu desktop, /etc/resolv.conf contains: nameserver 127.0.0.53. Which statement is correct?
o: It means no DNS server is set up, so name lookups fail
The stub resolver is running locally and works.
It is the address of the router, which must also serve DNS for the whole office
127.0.0.53 is a loopback address on this host, not a router.
The local stub resolver of systemd-resolved, which forwards upstream
Right. resolvectl status shows the actual upstream servers that the stub uses.
It is a typo and should be 127.0.0.1
127.0.0.53 is the standard address of the resolved stub.

q.q: Which TWO pairs of service and default port are correct? (Choose two.)
o: SMTP: TCP 25
Right. SMTP carries mail between servers on TCP port 25.
IMAP: TCP 110
TCP 110 is POP3. IMAP uses TCP 143.
HTTPS: TCP 80
TCP 80 is plain HTTP. HTTPS uses TCP 443.
NTP: UDP 123
Right. NTP uses UDP port 123 for time synchronization.
SSH: UDP 22
SSH runs over TCP port 22.

q.q: A security audit asks for a list of every regular file on the system that has the SUID bit set. Which command does it?
o: find / -type f -perm 4000 2>/dev/null
Without the minus sign, find matches only files whose mode is exactly 4000, which almost never exists.
find / -type f -perm -4000 2>/dev/null
Right. -perm -4000 matches files where the SUID bit is set, whatever the other bits are. The 2>/dev/null hides permission errors.
find / -type f -perm -2000 2>/dev/null
2000 is the SGID bit, not SUID.
find / -type f -user root -size +1 -perm 755 2>/dev/null
That lists files owned by root of a given size, and has nothing to do with the SUID bit.

q.q: Which command shows failed login attempts that were recorded in /var/log/btmp?
o: last -x
last reads wtmp and shows successful logins and reboots.
who
who shows who is logged in right now.
w
w shows who is logged in and what they are running, with no history of failures.
lastb
Right. lastb reads the btmp file of bad logins. It normally needs root.

q.q: An admin raises the open-file limit with ulimit -n 65535 in a terminal, then starts a daemon by a systemd unit. The daemon still hits a low limit. What is the best explanation?
o: ulimit -n only works for the root account, and not for any ordinary user account
Any user can lower a limit and may raise it up to the hard limit.
65535 is the maximum number of open files that the kernel allows on any system
The kernel allows much higher values, and the problem is where the limit is set.
It changes only that shell and its children; systemd units use LimitNOFILE
Right. A service started by systemd is not a child of the admin's terminal, so the new value does not reach it.
ulimit settings are cleared whenever a terminal prints output
Terminal output has no effect on limits.

q.q: Alice must be allowed to restart only the nginx service as root, and nothing else. Which /etc/sudoers line does that?
o: alice ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx
Right. The line gives one exact command with its full path. Alice can run just that line as root.
alice ALL=(ALL) ALL
This allows every command as any user, far more than needed.
alice ALL=(root) systemctl
sudoers needs the full path of the command, so visudo would flag this line. Even if it were accepted, every systemctl subcommand would be allowed.
alice ALL=NOPASSWD: /bin/bash
This gives her a root shell without a password, which defeats the point of limiting her.

q.q: Why is it better to change the sudo rules with visudo than with a normal text editor on /etc/sudoers?
o: visudo encrypts the sudoers file on disk so that users cannot read it
visudo does not encrypt anything.
visudo runs each edited rule as a test against every user on the machine
It checks the syntax. It does not run anything for users.
A normal editor cannot open files in /etc
Any editor can open it with root rights. The risk is saving a mistake.
It checks the syntax before saving, so one typo cannot lock everyone out of sudo
Right. A broken sudoers file can stop all sudo use. visudo refuses to save a file with errors.

q.q: An admin wants to run nmap against a whole company server range to find open ports. What must be in place first?
o: Written permission from the system owner, naming targets and dates
Right. Scanning without authorization can break policy and the law. Written scope protects both sides.
Nothing, because nmap only sends harmless pings and never touches services
nmap sends many probes, and unauthorized scanning can be a crime even if it is harmless.
An ICMP reply from each target
A reply shows a host is up. It does not give anyone permission to scan it.
The root password of every target
Credentials are not needed for a port scan, and they are no authorization either.

q.q: Which command shows the process that currently listens on TCP port 22?
o: lsof /dev/tcp/22
That is not a real path that lsof can use, so nothing useful is shown.
fuser /etc/ssh
fuser here would show processes using that folder, not the ones listening on port 22.
lsof -i TCP:22
Right. lsof lists open files and sockets. -i filters by network address, so it shows the sshd process.
who -p 22
who has no port option, and it lists logged-in users.

q.q: What is the difference between su alice and su - alice?
o: su - runs the shell without any password check for the target account
Both forms ask for the target user's password unless you are root.
su - gives her a full login environment; plain su keeps most of yours
Right. The dash gives a clean login shell as the target user. That includes her PATH and her startup files.
su alice works only while Alice has a session open on this system
su works for any valid account, logged in or not.
There is no difference, since the dash is ignored by the su command here
The dash changes the environment that the new shell gets.

q.q: An admin creates the empty file /etc/nologin before maintenance. What happens to ordinary users who try to log in?
o: Nothing, because the file must be named /etc/nologin.conf
The plain name /etc/nologin is the one checked by the login program.
All users, including root, are refused
root is explicitly allowed to log in so that the admin can finish the work.
Users who are already logged in are disconnected
The file affects new logins only. Existing sessions continue.
They are refused, and root can still log in
Right. While /etc/nologin exists, only root may log in. Its text is shown to the people who are turned away.

q.q: A service account named backup needs to own files and run jobs, but nobody should ever log in as it with a shell. Which is the best change?
o: Set its shell to /usr/sbin/nologin with usermod -s
Right. With that shell an interactive login is refused with a message, while cron jobs and files keep working.
Set its shell to /bin/bash and give it no password
That still allows other ways to log in, such as keys, and is the opposite of the goal.
Delete its entry from /etc/passwd
Files owned by the account would then show only a number and jobs would fail.
Move its home folder to /tmp
That does nothing about interactive logins and may lose data after a reboot.

q.q: A server has /etc/hosts.allow with the line sshd: 10.0.0. and /etc/hosts.deny with the line ALL: ALL, and sshd was built with TCP wrapper support. A client at 203.0.113.9 tries to connect over SSH. What happens?
o: The connection is allowed, because allow rules are checked first
Allow is checked first, but it only matches the 10.0.0. network, not this client.
The connection is allowed, because TCP wrappers apply only to telnet
They apply to any service that is built to use them, which includes sshd here.
Refused: no allow match, and the deny file matches everything
Right. hosts.allow is checked first, then hosts.deny. The first match decides, and no match means access is allowed.
The connection waits until an admin approves it
TCP wrappers have no approval step. They decide at once.

q.q: The telnet service runs under xinetd on an old server and must be turned off. What is the standard way?
o: Delete the line that mentions telnet from /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
That file lists accounts and has no list of services.
Set disable = yes in its xinetd.d file, then reload xinetd
Right. Each xinetd service has a file in that folder with a disable setting. A reload makes xinetd read it.
Add telnet to /etc/nologin
That file blocks logins during maintenance and does not select services.
Run ulimit -n 0 as root
That sets a limit in one shell and does not stop a service.

q.q: An admin stops cups.service and disables it, but a few minutes later CUPS is running again after a client connects to port 631. What should also be done?
o: Stop and disable cups.socket as well
Right. A systemd socket unit starts the service on demand, so the socket has to be disabled too.
Run systemctl unmask cups for the service
Unmasking would allow the service to run. It does not prevent it from starting.
Raise the nice value of cupsd
Priority has no influence on whether a service starts.
Edit /etc/inittab and add a respawn line for cupsd
A respawn line would make it restart automatically, which is the opposite.

q.q: After running ssh-keygen -t ed25519, which file is the one to copy to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server?
o: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
This is the private key. It must never leave the user's machine.
~/.ssh/known_hosts
That file lists the host keys of servers you connected to. It is not a login credential.
/etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key
That is the server's own private host key, never shared.
~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Right. The .pub file is the public half and is safe to share. ssh-copy-id installs it for you.

q.q: ssh refuses to use a key and prints WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE! Permissions 0644 for ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 are too open. What fixes it?
o: chmod 644 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
The public key's mode is not the problem.
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
Right. The private key must be readable by its owner only. 600 means read and write for the owner and nothing for others.
chmod 777 ~/.ssh
Opening the folder to everyone makes the problem worse, and sshd refuses a folder that others can write to.
chown root ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
A key owned by root can no longer be read by the user, so ssh fails differently.

q.q: When connecting to a server that the user has used for months, ssh prints WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! and stops. What is the best response?
o: Delete ~/.ssh entirely and reconnect
That throws away your own private keys and trusted hosts, and it does not answer the question of the changed key.
Use ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no to skip the warning for good
That turns off the very check that protects against a man-in-the-middle.
Confirm the key change with the admin first, then use ssh-keygen -R
Right. A changed host key may be a reinstall, or an attacker in the middle. Confirm out of band before trusting the new key.
Ignore it, because the warning only appears for new servers
The warning for a new server is a different message. This one means a known host presented a different key.

q.q: A user runs ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 and sees: Could not open a connection to your authentication agent. Which step is missing?
o: Run ssh-keygen -R localhost to clear the known_hosts entry
That removes an entry from known_hosts and does not start an agent.
Restart sshd on the remote server
The agent runs on the user's own machine, not on the server.
Start an agent with eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
Right. ssh-add talks to a running ssh-agent through environment variables, which the eval line sets.
Change the permissions of the key file to 777
A key that is open to everyone is rejected. The agent is simply not running.

q.q: A user runs: ssh -L 8080:intranet.example.com:80 alice@bastion.example.com and leaves it open. What can the user now do?
o: Let people on the intranet reach the user's local port 8080
That describes a remote forward (-R), which opens the port on the far side.
Use bastion.example.com as a SOCKS proxy on local port 8080
A SOCKS proxy is created with -D, not -L.
Copy files to the bastion with the same command
File copy uses scp or sftp. This command only sets up a tunnel.
Browse to http://localhost:8080 to reach the intranet site
Right. -L opens a local listening port whose traffic is carried through the SSH connection to the target.

q.q: Which ssh option creates a local SOCKS proxy on port 1080 that sends all proxied traffic through the SSH server?
o: ssh -L 1080 user@server
-L needs a target host and port, and it forwards one fixed destination.
ssh -D 1080 user@server
Right. -D means dynamic port forwarding. The local port acts as a SOCKS proxy.
ssh -R 1080 user@server
-R opens a port on the server that comes back to the client.
ssh -X 1080 user@server
-X turns on X11 forwarding and takes no port.

q.q: Alice wants to send a confidential file to Bob so that only Bob can read it. Which key does Alice use to encrypt it, and which key does Bob use to decrypt it?
o: Alice uses Bob's public key; Bob uses his private key
Right. Anyone may hold Bob's public key. Only his private key can open what it locked.
Alice encrypts with her private key; Bob decrypts with her public key
That describes a signature. Anybody with Alice's public key could read the data.
Alice encrypts with her public key; Bob decrypts with his public key
A public key cannot decrypt anything. Decryption needs the matching private key.
Both use the same shared secret stored in ~/.gnupg/
Public key encryption does not use a shared secret in that folder.

q.q: A project publishes release.tar.gz together with a detached signature release.tar.gz.sig. The signer's public key is already imported. Which command checks the download?
o: gpg --verify release.tar.gz.sig release.tar.gz
Right. gpg compares the signature to the file and reports if the signature is good and whose key made it.
gpg --decrypt release.tar.gz.sig
A detached signature holds no data to decrypt and does not check the other file.
gpg --import release.tar.gz.sig
--import adds keys to the keyring and a signature is not a key.
gpg --sign release.tar.gz
That creates a new signature with your own key, which proves nothing about the download.

q.q: A company cloned one VM image to twenty servers. Now every server shows the same SSH host key fingerprint. What is the right fix on each clone?
o: Copy the old server key to every user's authorized_keys file
authorized_keys is for user logins, and the problem is in the host keys.
Delete the ssh_host_* keys and generate new ones with ssh-keygen -A
Right. Each server needs its own host key so clients can tell servers apart. Restart sshd after the new keys exist.
Change PermitRootLogin to no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config on each clone
That limits root logins, and does nothing about duplicated host keys.
