Run ssh-keygen -R on each server
-R removes entries from known_hosts on the client, and keeps the duplicated host key.

q.q: An old server still has password hashes in the second field of /etc/passwd. Which command moves them into /etc/shadow?
o: pwunconv
pwunconv does the opposite. It moves hashes back into /etc/passwd, where every user can read them.
chpasswd -e
chpasswd sets passwords from a list of names and hashes. It does not move the stored ones.
passwd -x 90
-x sets the maximum age of a password and leaves where the hashes are stored unchanged.
pwconv
Right. pwconv creates /etc/shadow from /etc/passwd and replaces the hashes in the passwd file with an x.

q.q: Which TWO files does a TCP wrappers-enabled service read to decide whether a client may connect? (Choose two.)
o: /etc/hosts.allow
Right. It is checked first. A match here allows the client.
/etc/services
That file maps service names to ports and does not hold access rules.
/etc/nologin
That file blocks logins for non-root users during maintenance.
/etc/hosts.deny
Right. It is checked second. A match here refuses the client.
/etc/shadow
That file stores password hashes, not network access rules.

checks.why: The status and the syslog show cron starting run-parts for cron.daily at 06:25 with no error. So cron works, and the problem is in how run-parts treats this one script.

checks.t: Rename the script to a name without a dot

checks.t: Did not make the script world-writable

q.scenario: On ws12 you can reach the internet by address, but intranet.example.com does not resolve. Other workstations are fine. Find which DNS server ws12 is using, prove that it is the cause, and fix it in the way that survives a reboot. The correct DNS server is 10.0.0.2.

checks.why: NetworkManager builds /etc/resolv.conf from the profile, so nmcli con mod office-lan ipv4.dns 10.0.0.2 changes the source and is saved across reboots.

checks.t: Bring the connection up again so the change takes effect

q.title: Bob's SSH key is ignored
q.scenario: Bob's public key was added to srv01, but ssh still asks him for a password. Find out why the server ignores the key and fix it. Keep key login working the safe way: do not weaken the SSH server settings.
q.ticket: INC-6188: bob (laptop 10.20.10.51) cannot use key login to srv01 (Debian 12). His key line is already in /home/bob/.ssh/authorized_keys. Everything in /home/bob belongs to bob.
q.intro: srv01 (Debian 12). You are logged in as an admin with sudo. Type help to see the commands.

checks.t: Read why sshd rejected the key (log)
checks.why: The log says: Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes for file /home/bob/.ssh/authorized_keys. sshd names the exact cause, then lets Bob fall back to his password.

checks.t: Look at the permissions of the .ssh folder and key file
checks.why: ls -ld shows drwxrwxrwx on .ssh and -rw-rw-rw- on authorized_keys. Both are writable by every user. sshd's StrictModes check refuses keys in such places.

checks.t: Remove group and other write access from the .ssh folder
checks.why: chmod 700 gives the owner full access and nobody else any. If others could write to the folder, they could swap in their own key and log in as Bob.

checks.t: Remove group and other write access from authorized_keys
checks.why: chmod 600 (or 644) keeps others from editing the key list. A file anyone can change would let anyone add a key for Bob's account.

checks.t: Look at the permissions again to confirm
checks.why: After the fix, neither the folder nor the file should be writable by group or others (for example drwx------ and -rw-------). A look taken before the fix shows the old values.

checks.t: Did not switch off StrictModes
checks.why: StrictModes yes is the safe default. Turning it off hides the problem for everybody and lets badly protected key files work on the whole server.

checks.t: Did not open the files to everyone
checks.why: The files were already too open. Making them 777 (or 666) is the cause of the failure, not the cure.

q.title: Read the SSH log: which lines are a problem?
q.scenario: You are the on-call admin for web01. Read these lines from /var/log/auth.log. Mark every line where the attacker tried to log in or succeeded (failed guesses and the Accepted line). Do not mark the login manager's own session record. Then choose what to do next.
q.ticket: Alert: more than 100 failed SSH logins on web01 in 5 minutes. Admins connect only from the 10.20.10.0/24 office network. 198.51.100.23 is an outside address.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:11:48 web01 sshd[2201]: Accepted publickey for gdavis from 10.20.10.44 port 50122 ssh2: ED25519 SHA256:Qm4x...
lines.why: A normal key login by the admin from the office network. Nothing here is out of place.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:12:44 web01 sshd[2310]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 198.51.100.23 port 40122 ssh2
lines.why: An outside address tries a user name that does not exist on the machine. Guessing common names like admin is a typical password-guessing attack.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:12:46 web01 sshd[2312]: Failed password for root from 198.51.100.23 port 40130 ssh2
lines.why: The same outside address now tries root. Many failures from one source in seconds point to an automated attack.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:12:49 web01 CRON[2320]: pam_unix(cron:session): session opened for user root(uid=0) by (uid=0)
lines.why: Cron opens a session to run a scheduled job. This is routine and has no network source.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:12:51 web01 sshd[2331]: Failed password for invalid user oracle from 198.51.100.23 port 40144 ssh2
lines.why: A third guess from the same address with another common account name. The pattern is a dictionary-style attack.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:13:02 web01 sshd[2340]: pam_unix(sshd:auth): authentication failure; logname= uid=0 euid=0 tty=ssh ruser= rhost=198.51.100.23  user=bob
lines.why: PAM records a failed password for the real account bob, from the same outside address. The attacker is now trying real user names.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:13:09 web01 sshd[2342]: Accepted password for bob from 198.51.100.23 port 40190 ssh2
lines.why: The most important line. After the failures, the outside address got in as bob with a password. Treat the account as compromised.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:13:09 web01 systemd-logind[701]: New session 41 of user bob.
lines.why: This is the normal login manager record of the session. It is the result of the line above, but it does not show an attack by itself.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:15:30 web01 sudo: gdavis : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/home/gdavis ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/apt update
lines.why: The admin ran a normal sudo command from his own session. It is expected maintenance.

lines.text: Nov 27 03:16:12 web01 sshd[2410]: Disconnected from user gdavis 10.20.10.44 port 50122
lines.why: The admin's own session ended. It is a normal log entry.

ask.label: What is the best next step?
opts: Do nothing, because failed logins from the internet are only normal background noise
Restart sshd so that the failed login counters and the open sessions are reset
Treat bob as compromised: lock him out, end his session, start incident response
Delete /var/log/auth.log so the attack stops filling the log and the disk
ask.why: One of the outside guesses worked, so an attacker may be inside as bob. Lock the account, end the session, keep the logs as evidence and follow your incident process. Restarting or deleting logs removes evidence and fixes nothing.

q.title: Create a contractor account that expires
q.scenario: A contractor, J. Lee, needs a normal login account called jlee until 2027-03-31. The group contractors does not exist yet. She must choose her own password at first login. Build the commands in the right order and leave out the ones that do not belong.
q.ticket: Request HR-3321, approved by the system owner. Run the commands as root on files01. The account must have a home folder and use bash.

rules.why: The group must exist before an account can use it as its primary group. useradd stops with an error if the group is missing.
-m makes the home folder, -s sets bash, -g sets the primary group and -e sets the date on which the account expires.
A new account has no usable password. Setting a first password gives her something to log in with.
Setting the last-change date to 0 forces a new password at first login. It must come after passwd, because passwd sets the change date to today and would undo it.
Lists the aging data, so you can confirm the expiry date of 2027-03-31 and that a password change is required.
-L locks the password, so she could not log in with it. It is the opposite of what the ticket asks.
-r creates a system account with a low UID and no home folder or aging rules. A contractor needs a normal account.
UID 0 is root. This would hand her full control of the machine, and editing the file by hand skips safety checks.
This deletes the account and its home folder. It is the clean-up for the end of the contract, not for the start.

before.why: useradd -g contractors needs the group to exist already, so groupadd comes first.
passwd works on an account that already exists, so the account must be created first.
passwd resets the last-change date to today. Run chage -d 0 afterwards, or the forced change at first login is lost.

last.why: A final look with chage -l confirms the whole result, so it is the last step.

q.title: Follow a message from the mail command to the remote server
q.scenario: On app01 (running Postfix) Alice types: mail -s Report bob@example.org. The remote domain is reachable over the internet. Place each stage in the order the message passes through it.

devs.name: mail command (mail user agent)
devs.why: The mail command lets a person write a message. It does not deliver anything itself. It hands the message over.

devs.name: sendmail-compatible command from Postfix
devs.why: mail passes the message to /usr/sbin/sendmail. Postfix provides this command, so the same call works with any MTA.

devs.name: Mail queue (shown by mailq)
devs.why: Postfix first stores the message in its queue. mailq lists what is waiting, and deferred messages are retried from here.

devs.name: DNS MX lookup for example.org
devs.why: The MTA asks DNS which mail server accepts mail for example.org. MX records give that name.

devs.name: SMTP session to the remote MTA, TCP 25
devs.why: Server-to-server mail is sent over SMTP on TCP port 25. The remote MTA then stores it in Bob's mailbox.

devs.name: ~/.forward file of bob
devs.why: A .forward file is read on the receiving host when mail is delivered locally, and the recipient here is on another domain.

devs.name: IMAP server (Dovecot) on app01
devs.why: IMAP lets a user read stored mail. It plays no part in sending a message to another domain.

devs.name: CUPS print spool
devs.why: CUPS queues print jobs. It has nothing to do with mail.
